terms.definition: The chip that actually carries out a program's instructions — fetching one, figuring out what it means, doing it, and repeating, billions of times per second. It's the part of the computer that thinks.

One independent worker inside a CPU chip that can run its own stream of instructions. Modern CPUs bundle several of these together so multiple things can genuinely happen at the exact same instant, not just take turns quickly.

How many timing 'ticks' per second a CPU's internal clock generates — measured in GHz (billions of ticks per second). More ticks generally means more work done per second, but a chip's internal design matters too, so clock speed alone doesn't decide performance.

A small pocket of extremely fast memory built right onto the CPU chip, holding data the CPU recently used or expects to need again soon — so it doesn't have to wait on much slower main memory (RAM) for everything.
The computer's fast, temporary working memory — it holds whatever is actively being used right now, but its contents vanish the instant power is lost. That fragility is the tradeoff for its speed.
A drive (SSD or HDD) that keeps data even with no power at all — that's why your files are still there after a shutdown — in exchange for being much slower to access than RAM.

Memory is 'volatile' if it needs continuous power to hold its contents (like RAM) and 'non-volatile' if it keeps data with no power at all (like an SSD or HDD). This is a precise technical distinction, not a loose figure of speech.

The main circuit board that every other core part — CPU, RAM, storage, GPU — physically plugs into, and which carries every signal between them. Without it, those parts are just isolated chips with no way to talk to each other.

A physical set of electrical pathways on the motherboard that carries data and control signals between components — different buses (like the memory bus or PCIe) handle different jobs at different speeds.
A set of supporting chips on the motherboard that manages traffic between the CPU and the rest of the system, so the CPU isn't stuck personally handling every peripheral interaction.

A chip built with thousands of simple cores that all run the same operation on different pieces of data at once — great for graphics rendering and, it turns out, the exact math behind training AI models.

Running the same simple calculation on many pieces of data at the exact same time, rather than working through them one at a time. This only pays off when a task can be broken into many independent, identical steps.

A solid-state electronic switch with no moving parts — it's either ON (letting current through) or OFF (blocking it), controlled by a small voltage. It's the single physical building block every digital computation ultimately rests on.

A small circuit built from a handful of transistors that takes binary inputs (1s and 0s) and produces one output according to a fixed rule — AND, OR, and NOT are the three basic types, and everything else is built by combining them.
A number system with only two digits, 0 and 1, instead of decimal's ten. Computers use it because a transistor only reliably has two distinguishable states — current flowing or not.
The smallest unit of information a computer can store — a single binary digit, 0 or 1. Every file, program, and piece of data you'll ever touch is, underneath, a long precise sequence of these.

An agreed-upon scheme for turning binary numbers into readable text — ASCII is an older, smaller standard; Unicode/UTF-8 is the modern standard covering nearly every writing system and symbol, including emoji.
The electrical 'pressure' pushing electrons to flow between two points — like water pressure in a pipe. A binary 1 or 0 is really just a high or low voltage measured at a specific instant.
The actual rate electrons are flowing past a point in a circuit — like the volume of water moving through a pipe, as opposed to voltage, which is the pressure pushing it.
Software that's permanently paired with one specific piece of hardware, stored on a small chip built into it, handling that hardware's most basic startup behavior before any operating system exists.

The firmware built into the motherboard that runs the instant you hit the power button, before anything else — it checks that core hardware works, then hands off to the operating system. UEFI is the modern, faster, more secure replacement for the older BIOS.
terms.technical_term: BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) / UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface)

terms.definition: A fixed sequence of hardware checks that BIOS/UEFI runs the instant you power on, confirming the CPU, RAM, and other essentials are present and working before anything else happens.
A UEFI feature that cryptographically checks the bootloader hasn't been tampered with before letting it run — a real defense against malware that tries to infect the startup process itself.
A small program, loaded by the firmware, whose only job is finding and loading the much larger operating system kernel into RAM.
The core part of an operating system that directly manages hardware resources, memory, and running processes — everything else the OS does builds on top of it.
A small piece of software written to let the OS communicate with one specific type of hardware, like a disk controller or network adapter.

The fixed, ordered sequence a computer follows getting from fully off to a usable desktop — firmware runs, hardware is checked, a bootloader loads the kernel, drivers and services start, and finally the desktop appears.

The software layer between raw hardware and every application, hiding hardware's messy details behind a consistent interface apps can rely on — like a hotel manager handling the building's plumbing so guests don't have to.

A running instance of a program with its own private, isolated chunk of memory that other processes can't directly read or write — that isolation is what stops one crashing app from corrupting another.

A sequence of instructions running inside a process. Multiple threads in the same process share that process's memory, which makes them fast to coordinate but risks two threads stepping on the same data at once.
A bug where two threads sharing the same memory corrupt each other's data because they weren't carefully coordinated about who touches it and when.

The OS rapidly saving one thread's current state, loading another thread's state onto a core, and resuming it — done so fast, many times a second, that programs appear to run simultaneously even on limited cores.

The OS's job of deciding what data occupies RAM at any moment, since RAM is limited and shared. When demand outgrows RAM, the OS borrows storage space as overflow — virtual memory — which is much slower.
The area of a storage drive the OS uses as overflow memory when RAM fills up — called a page file on Windows, a swap file/partition on Mac/Linux.
The organizational scheme (like NTFS, APFS, or ext4) an OS uses to track every file's name, size, location, and permissions on a drive — like a library's card catalog for raw data.
Information about a file — its name, size, timestamps, permissions — that the file system tracks separately from the file's actual content.
Not a physical container — just an entry in the file system that groups references to other files and folders together for organization and lookup.

The address of a file within a file system. An absolute path spells out the full route from the drive's root; a relative path is measured from wherever you currently are, which makes it shorter but only meaningful relative to a starting point.
The folder a terminal session or program is currently 'standing in' — every relative path you type is interpreted starting from here.

A text-based way of controlling a computer — type an instruction, press enter, it runs. It came first historically, before graphics were practical, and never disappeared because it's fast, scriptable, and often the only interface a server has.
The icons, windows, and pointer-driven interaction most people associate with using a computer — became standard once displays and processing power made rendering graphics affordable.
A saved sequence of terminal commands that can be run all at once, automatically, with no further human input needed.
The actual program that reads what you type into a terminal, figures out what command it means, and carries it out. The terminal is the window; the shell is the program doing the real work inside it.

A real, physical network of independently owned networks — fiber cables, wireless links, satellites — all agreeing to communicate using shared protocols. No single company or computer runs the whole thing.

A precisely defined, standardized set of rules for how data is formatted, addressed, and exchanged between devices — so any two devices following the same protocol can understand each other, regardless of who made them.
The internet's foundational set of protocols, defining how data gets broken into pieces, addressed, routed, and reassembled correctly at its destination.

A numerical identifier assigned to a device on a network, so data knows exactly which machine it's meant for — like a mailing address on an envelope. IPv6 exists because IPv4 was running out of unique addresses.
Whatever initiates a request for data or a service — your browser asking for a webpage, an app asking for updated data. It sends a request and waits for a response.
Software (usually running on a dedicated machine) that listens for incoming requests and responds to them — like a kitchen preparing what a waiter (the client) asked for.
A large, specialized facility built to house huge numbers of servers with reliable power, cooling, and network connectivity.
Despite the weightless-sounding name, just servers in a data center you access remotely over the internet instead of running the equivalent hardware yourself — 'someone else's computer,' rented.
The system that translates human-readable names like google.com into the numerical IP addresses computers actually need to find each other — like a phone book.
The human-readable name (like google.com) that DNS translates into the actual numerical IP address needed to make a connection.
A program as a human programmer writes and reads it — structured, at least somewhat readable logic. A CPU can't run this directly; it has to first become machine code.
The low-level, binary format a CPU can actually execute directly — sequences of numbers corresponding to primitive operations the hardware physically knows how to do.
The process of turning source code into machine code — either all at once ahead of time (compilation) or one instruction at a time as the program runs (interpretation).
The standardized rules governing how a browser's request and a server's response must be formatted, so any browser can talk to any web server correctly.
Software built to run directly on a specific operating system, using its own interfaces to interact with hardware — often more efficient than something running inside a browser.
Software that looks and feels like a native app but actually runs inside a browser tab, built with web technologies and constantly talking to a server in the background.
A newer version of a program's code, released to fix bugs, close security holes, or add new features — installing one replaces some or all of the previously installed files.
A specific flaw in a program's code that an attacker could exploit to do something the program was never meant to allow — patching a known one is usually treated as urgent.
A stiff paper card with a pattern of holes representing instructions or data, used to program and feed data into early computers before keyboards and screens existed.
A sealed glass tube used as the earliest electronic on/off switch in computing, before transistors — bulky, fragile, power-hungry, and prone to burning out.

Many transistors, already wired together, fabricated directly onto a single piece of silicon — the direct ancestor of every modern CPU, letting transistor counts scale with manufacturing precision instead of hand-wiring.

Submitting a complete, fixed set of instructions and waiting for results with no way to interact partway through — the old punch-card model, replaced by interactive computing (type something, see an immediate response) once keyboards and monitors arrived.

Breaking data into small, independently addressed chunks (packets) that can each travel by whatever path is available and be reassembled at the destination — if one path fails, packets just reroute instead of the whole communication failing.

Web pages, hyperlinks, and browsers, built by Tim Berners-Lee on top of the internet's already-existing infrastructure — the furniture built on top of the internet's plumbing, not the plumbing itself.

A machine learning technique loosely modeled on how biological neurons connect, organized into layers that progressively transform input data into an output prediction — the dominant approach behind modern AI.

Rather than a human hand-writing rules, a program is given a lot of example data and works out patterns on its own — a fundamentally different approach than the hand-coded rule-based AI of earlier decades.
A very large-scale neural network trained on enormous amounts of text, learning to predict and generate coherent language — the technology behind systems like GPT and Claude.

A material (like silicon) whose ability to conduct electricity sits between a conductor (lets current flow freely) and an insulator (blocks it almost entirely) — and, crucially, can be controlled on demand, which is exactly what a switch needs.

Deliberately introducing tiny amounts of other elements into silicon to precisely change how it conducts electricity, creating n-type or p-type regions. Joining these forms a p-n junction, whose current flow can be switched on or off by voltage — the physical mechanism behind a transistor.
A negatively charged subatomic particle — its movement through a conductive material is what electricity physically is.
A complete, closed loop that electric current can flow through. Break the loop anywhere — with a switch or a transistor — and current stops flowing entirely.
A signal that can take on any value across a smooth, continuous range, with no fixed steps — like a dimmer switch that can be set anywhere along its slider.

A signal that only takes on a fixed, limited set of distinct values — in computing, almost always just 1 and 0. Real-world analog signals like sound get converted into digital form by sampling: measuring the value at many fixed instants per second.
How many complete cycles of a repeating wave happen in one second, measured in Hertz (Hz) — a CPU's clock speed, in GHz, is just frequency measured in billions of cycles per second.

The type of transistor used in most modern chips, with three terminals — source, drain, and gate. Voltage on the gate creates an electric field that opens or closes a conductive channel between source and drain, with zero moving parts.

Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of transistors fitting on a chip of a given size would roughly double every two years — held true for decades and is why CPUs kept getting dramatically more capable.

An extraordinarily precise, extremely expensive facility where chips are physically manufactured — silicon is sliced into wafers, then patterned with photolithography (projecting light through a stencil-like mask) to define where transistors form.

A memory chip built to hold data reliably without needing constant power, and without being casually overwritten the way a regular file can be. Firmware lives in a chip like this. (A separate, older use of the same abbreviation shows up for old game cartridges — see 'ROM dump'.)
Two competing schemes for organizing a drive's partitions. GPT is the modern one UEFI uses, supporting drives over 2TB and more partitions; MBR is the older, more limited scheme classic BIOS used.
terms.technical_term: GUID Partition Table (GPT) / Master Boot Record (MBR)

terms.definition: A special startup mode where the OS deliberately loads only a minimal set of essential drivers and skips most startup programs — useful for diagnosing a problem caused by something that normally loads automatically.

The short suffix at the end of a filename (like .jpg or .docx) hinting at what's inside. It's mostly a trusted convention, not a technical guarantee — the OS doesn't inspect the actual bytes every time you double-click a file.

A short sequence of bytes at the very start of a file that identifies its real format, regardless of whatever extension is attached to the filename — how tools can detect a deliberately mislabeled file.
A file structure (like .mp4 or .mkv) that bundles video, audio, subtitles, and metadata together into one file. The container is the box; it says nothing on its own about what codec is inside.
The specific algorithm used to compress raw video or audio down to a much smaller size, and decompress it back for playback. Two files in the same container can use completely different codecs.
A single file that bundles multiple files and folders together while preserving their individual identities, usually paired with compression to shrink the result.

Lossless compression shrinks data with zero information lost — every original byte can be reconstructed exactly. Lossy compression (used by most video/audio codecs) permanently discards some data for a much bigger size reduction.
An exact, byte-for-byte digital copy of everything on a physical disc, packed into a single file — can be mounted or burned to recreate the original disc's contents and structure.

A digital file capturing a game cartridge's memory chip contents byte by byte, played back by an emulator — a program that simulates the original hardware well enough to run it on completely different hardware.
A device that examines an incoming packet's destination address and forwards it toward the next network hop on its journey — sitting at nearly every junction point across the internet.
A company that operates the physical infrastructure connecting homes and businesses to the wider internet, and connects in turn to other ISPs and larger backbone providers.
The process a home router uses to translate between many private IP addresses inside a house and the single public IP address representing that household to the outside internet.
A service, usually built into a home router, that automatically hands out private IP addresses to devices the instant they join a network — no manual configuration required.
A wireless networking technology that lets devices connect to a local network using radio waves instead of physical cables, governed by the 802.11 technical standard.
The encryption standard that scrambles data traveling between a device and a router so anyone else nearby, without the password, can't meaningfully read the traffic.

A short-range wireless technology for direct, one-to-one connections between nearby devices, with no router involved — optimized for low power rather than network connectivity. BLE is a variant built for devices that only send small amounts of data occasionally.
A numbered communication channel layered on top of an IP address, identifying a specific program on a device — letting one IP address host many simultaneous conversations at once.

TCP is a reliable, ordered protocol that guarantees every packet arrives and resends any that don't. UDP skips that overhead for speed, with no guarantee a packet arrives at all — the tradeoff between correctness and speed.

A unique identifier permanently burned into a specific piece of network hardware, unlike an IP address which changes as a device moves between networks. ARP is the process a device uses to look up which MAC address matches a given IP address on its local network.
A generational leap in cellular network technology — new radio equipment, new licensed spectrum, and new phone hardware — each one substantially increasing speed and reducing latency over the last.

A layered model organizing the whole journey data takes across a network — physical, link, network, transport, and application layers — each one handling a different piece of getting data to the right place.

A website specifically built to feel and behave more like a native app — installable to a home screen, capable of some offline functionality — while still fundamentally running through a browser's rendering engine.

Charles Babbage's 1830s design for a general-purpose mechanical computer — a 'mill' for arithmetic, a 'store' for memory, and punched cards for changeable instructions — never actually built at the time due to manufacturing limits.
A hardware design whose technical specifications are published rather than kept secret, letting other manufacturers build compatible machines — the approach IBM took with the 1981 IBM PC.
A mobile phone that evolved into a genuinely full, general-purpose computer — running a real OS, real installed apps, and constant internet connectivity — distributed through a centralized app store.
The equation V = I × R relating voltage, current, and resistance — the precise mathematical version of 'more voltage pushes more current through a fixed resistance.'
The physical distance a wave travels over one complete cycle. For waves traveling at a fixed speed, wavelength and frequency are inversely related — higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

A transistor design pairing NMOS and PMOS transistors together so current only flows briefly during switching, not continuously while idle — the dominant, power-efficient design used throughout the chip industry.

The one repeating cycle every computer is built around, at every scale — input comes in, processing transforms it, output goes back out, and storage lets some of that data outlive the moment it was created.

The unavoidable energy wasted as heat every time a transistor switches state. With billions of switches happening every second, that tiny per-switch waste adds up to real heat output — exactly why CPUs and GPUs need active cooling.

A non-volatile, electrically-based memory technology that stores each bit by trapping or releasing an electrical charge inside a specially built transistor cell, with no moving parts. It's the underlying technology an SSD is built from.

Logic built into SSD firmware that deliberately spreads writes evenly across all of a drive's flash memory cells, rather than repeatedly hammering the same location — extending the drive's usable lifespan, since each cell can only be written to a finite number of times.
A standardized physical connector and communication protocol that lets wildly different devices — keyboards, mice, drives, chargers — all connect through one shared port and cable design.
Any hardware that lets a computer exchange data with the outside world — a keyboard and mouse send data in, a monitor and speakers send data back out, and some devices (a touchscreen) do both.

The ability to connect or disconnect a device while the computer is fully powered on and running, with the OS detecting the change immediately rather than requiring a restart — something USB was deliberately designed around.
The smallest individually controllable unit of a display, capable of showing one specific color at any instant by combining red, green, and blue light in different proportions.
The total count of pixels a display contains, expressed as width by height — more pixels means more spatial detail a still image can contain at any single instant.

How many times per second a display redraws its entire image from scratch, measured in Hertz. It's a hard ceiling on how much of a GPU's rendered output can actually be shown, no matter how many frames per second the GPU produces.

How quickly an individual pixel can finish physically changing from one color to another — a separate property from refresh rate; a high refresh rate on paper can still show visible blur if the panel's response time is slow.

A formal, strictly-defined system of grammar and meaning that lets a person write instructions precise enough for a machine to carry out — unlike everyday English, a missing comma or bracket can make the whole thing fail.

The large collection of pre-written, ready-to-use functionality that ships alongside a language itself, so a programmer isn't forced to build basic capabilities like math or text handling from scratch.
A compact, partially-translated form of a program that sits between raw human-readable source code and the CPU's own native machine code — not quite either one.

A hybrid translation strategy where a program watches itself run and compiles its most frequently executed pieces into genuine native machine code on the fly, mid-execution, rather than all at once beforehand or one line at a time forever.

A structured internal representation of a program's actual grammatical relationships — which instructions nest inside which — built from source code during translation, independent of its exact original formatting.
Runtime is the period a program is actually executing; compile time is the earlier phase when source code is being translated. Some errors only ever show up at one of the two, never the other.
A name a programmer assigns to a specific location in memory, letting code refer to stored data by a readable label instead of a raw address.
The rule specifying what kind of value a variable holds and, critically, what operations are actually valid to perform on it — adding two integers differs completely from "adding" two strings.
A statically typed language checks a variable's type before the program ever runs; a dynamically typed language checks types at runtime instead, letting a variable's type shift more freely.

Deliberately or automatically moving a value from one data type to another — explicit conversion is requested on purpose; implicit conversion (coercion) happens silently and is a common source of subtle bugs.

A value type stores its actual data directly at a variable's own memory location; a reference type instead stores a pointer to where the real data lives elsewhere — copying one gives an independent copy, copying the other gives two labels pointing at the same data.

A background process, built into many language runtimes, that automatically identifies memory no longer reachable by any variable in the program and reclaims it for reuse, without the programmer manually tracking and releasing it.
A symbol — like +, ==, or && — that performs a specific operation on one or more values (operands) and produces a result, falling into arithmetic, comparison, logical, and assignment categories.
The rules determining which operators get evaluated first when several appear in one expression — directly analogous to standard math's order of operations.

Skipping evaluation of a logical expression's second condition once the first has already determined the overall result — an AND stops once the first side is false, an OR stops once the first side is true.

A piece of code that runs a specific block only if a given condition evaluates to true, and optionally a different block if it evaluates to false — a real, physical branch in which instructions the CPU executes next.

A structure comparing one single value against a list of possible exact matches, running whichever block belongs to the matching case — a more readable alternative to a long else-if chain for this one specific situation.

A control structure that repeatedly executes a block of code as long as, or until, some condition is met — mechanically just a conditional combined with an instruction to jump backward in the program's own instructions.
A loop whose continuation condition never actually becomes false, so it keeps executing forever, or until the program is forcibly stopped or crashes from resource exhaustion.
A loop or array access written to run, or reach, one time too many or too few relative to what was actually intended — the single most common mistake programmers make with loops and indexing.

A named, reusable block of code performing a specific task, invokable from elsewhere in a program as many times as needed, optionally accepting input (parameters) and producing an output (a return value).

A parameter is the named placeholder a function's own definition declares it will accept; an argument is the actual specific value supplied at the moment the function is called to fill that placeholder in.

The set of rules determining where in a program a given variable is actually visible and usable — a local variable is only visible inside the function that declares it; a global variable is visible from anywhere.

A specific memory region tracking, in order, every function currently in the middle of running, so that when an inner function finishes, execution correctly resumes exactly where the outer, calling code left off.
Text a programmer deliberately writes into source code that the compiler or interpreter completely ignores — invisible to the running program, existing purely for human readers.

A specially formatted comment placed at the start of a function, following a language-specific convention that lets tools automatically extract and display it, without a reader needing to open the function's actual code.
A precise, ordered sequence of steps for solving a specific problem or accomplishing a specific task — the same basic shape as a recipe, just applied to computation instead of cooking.
Writing out an algorithm's logic using plain, structured language that resembles real code's shape, without committing to any one specific programming language's exact syntax rules.

A visual representation of an algorithm's logic as connected shapes — typically a diamond for a decision, a rectangle for a processing step, and arrows showing order — capturing the same structure pseudocode does, just visually.
A violation of a programming language's grammar rules, caught before the program ever actually runs — the translation process simply can't proceed with grammatically invalid input.

An error that occurs while a program is actually executing — the code was grammatically valid and successfully translated, but encounters a specific situation, like dividing by zero, it can't handle correctly mid-execution.

The most insidious error category: code runs successfully from start to finish with no error message at all, but produces an incorrect result because the underlying logic itself doesn't do what was intended.

A specialized tool that lets a programmer pause a running program at a specific line and inspect the actual current values of variables at that exact moment — directly observing behavior instead of guessing at it.
A printed report showing the exact chain of function calls active at the moment an error occurred, letting a programmer trace exactly how execution arrived at the failing line.

A package is a bundle of pre-written code published for reuse; a dependency is a package a project relies on to function; a package manager is the tool that automates finding, installing, and tracking them.

A manifest file lists which packages a project depends on, sometimes within a flexible version range; a lockfile records the exact, specific version of every dependency actually installed at one particular moment, for reliable recreation later.

A high-level language abstracts away hardware detail, letting a programmer write in terms close to human logic; a low-level language exposes program logic close to what the hardware actually does, offering precise but manual control.

A variable that directly stores a memory address — the actual physical location of another piece of data — rather than storing a value itself, giving a programmer explicit, direct access to where data lives in RAM.

A fundamental style or philosophy for structuring and organizing code, not a specific language — imperative programming is an explicit step-by-step sequence changing state; object-oriented programming bundles data and behavior into objects.
A class is the blueprint defining what data and behavior objects created from it will have; an object (or instance) is one specific, concrete thing actually created from that blueprint.

A word reserved by a language's own syntax rules for a specific, fixed meaning — like if, while, or return — which can't be reused as a variable name because doing so would create genuine semantic ambiguity.

A single, compact, highly readable line for building a new list from an existing one — syntactic sugar for the same loop-and-append logic, just condensed into a form that reads almost like plain English.

Python's own official, widely-followed style guide — recommended conventions for naming, spacing, and organizing code that aren't strictly enforced by the language itself but are broadly adopted across the community.
JavaScript’s == performs loose equality, allowing type conversion before comparing (5 == "5" is true); === performs strict equality, requiring both value and type to match with no conversion at all.

A mechanism that lets slow operations, like fetching data from a server, run in the background without freezing an entire page, resuming a specific piece of code once that slower operation actually finishes.

The browser's own structured internal representation of a page's HTML content, which JavaScript is given direct, programmatic access to read and modify, with the browser automatically re-rendering the visible page to match.
A runtime environment that lets JavaScript execute as a genuine backend server language, not just inside browser-rendered pages, meaningfully expanding where JavaScript can actually be used.

A program built to interpret, or further just-in-time compile, Java's own bytecode into whatever a specific local machine's native instructions genuinely are — the platform-specific piece making "write once, run anywhere" work.

A category of runtime error Java's compiler forces a programmer to explicitly acknowledge and handle before the program is even allowed to compile, pulling a known failure mode partway into compile-time visibility.

A file declaring what functions and data a piece of C or C++ code makes available, separate from the actual implementation file, letting the compiler check usage without needing the full implementation present.
Forgetting to release memory that's no longer needed — a real category of bug manual memory management introduces that a garbage-collected language mostly prevents automatically.

C#'s direct architectural parallel to Java's JVM/bytecode pair — C# source compiles to CIL, an intermediate representation, which then runs on the CLR, translating it into the local machine's actual native instructions.
terms.technical_term: Common Language Runtime (CLR) / Common Intermediate Language (CIL)

terms.definition: Language Integrated Query — a C# feature letting a programmer write SQL-like query syntax directly inside C# code itself, to filter, sort, and transform data.

An error occurring when code attempts to use a reference-type variable that doesn't actually point at any real data at all — a longstanding, common bug modern C# lets a programmer flag and check for at compile time.
terms.technical_term: Null Reference Error / Nullable Reference Type

terms.definition: A language, like SQL, that specifies what result is wanted rather than an exact step-by-step procedure for reaching it, leaving the actual execution strategy to a separate engine.
DDL commands define and modify a database's structure (creating tables and columns); DML commands work with the data already living inside that structure (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).
terms.technical_term: DDL (Data Definition Language) / DML (Data Manipulation Language)

terms.definition: A SQL operation combining rows from two separate, related tables based on a shared identifier, letting a single query pull together data that's deliberately stored separately for organizational reasons.

The part of a database engine that decides the actual, specific execution strategy for a declarative query — potentially using an index or another efficient retrieval strategy the query itself never specifies.
A language, like HTML, that structures and describes content rather than expressing logic or computation — marking pieces of content as headings, paragraphs, or links using nested tags.

The concept every HTML element's layout is built around: content surrounded by padding, a border, and margin, four concentric layers nearly every CSS layout rule is ultimately manipulating some combination of.

Writing CSS that adapts a page's layout appropriately across different screen sizes, commonly using media queries — CSS rules that apply only when the browser's viewport meets specific size conditions.

A structured, opinionated toolkit built on top of plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, providing reusable patterns and pre-built tooling for constructing complex, interactive user interfaces more manageably.

A reusable, self-contained piece of a user interface, bundling its own structure, styling, and behavior into one cohesive unit — the central concept nearly every modern frontend framework is built around.
A framework automatically detecting when a component's underlying data has changed and efficiently re-rendering exactly the specific, affected parts of the page that actually need updating.
An ordered collection of values stored under one name and accessed by numeric position, called an index — most languages use zero-based indexing, where the first element sits at index 0, not 1.

A fixed-size array has its total capacity set once, upfront; a dynamic array can grow and shrink as needed, automatically allocating a larger block and copying elements over when it runs out of reserved space.
A collection of key-value pairs, where each unique key maps directly to one specific associated value, looked up by that key rather than by any numeric position.

Union combines two sets into one with every value from either; intersection keeps only values present in both; difference keeps values in one set but not the other; symmetric difference keeps values in exactly one.
A data structure following LIFO order (Last In, First Out) — the most recently added item is always the first one removed, supporting push (add to the top) and pop (remove from the top).
A data structure following FIFO order (First In, First Out) — the earliest-added item is always the first one removed, supporting enqueue (add to the back) and dequeue (remove from the front).
A hybrid structure allowing items to be added and removed from both ends at once, letting it behave exactly like a stack, exactly like a queue, or something genuinely more flexible than either.

A structure made of individual nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node in the sequence, scattered anywhere in memory rather than sitting contiguously — a doubly linked list adds a "previous" pointer too.

A structure using a hash function — which deterministically turns a key into a number — to decide exactly where in an underlying array a key's data should be stored, so lookup doesn't require searching item by item.
terms.technical_term: Hash Table / Hash Function / Collision / Bucket

terms.definition: JavaScript Object Notation — a lightweight, text-based data format for representing structured data (objects and arrays) using a simple syntax essentially every modern programming language can both read and write.
Comma-Separated Values — a plain-text format representing tabular data, where each line is one row and individual values are separated by a delimiter, commonly a comma.

A reference a program uses for every subsequent read or write on a specific file, obtained by asking the OS to open it; buffering means written data may sit temporarily in memory before actually reaching disk.

A formal definition specifying the expected structure of a piece of data — which fields must be present, what type each is, and what constraints apply — letting incoming data be validated against it immediately.

Converting a program's own in-memory data structure into a format that can be stored or transmitted, like JSON or CSV; deserialization is the reverse, reconstructing that data back into a usable in-memory structure.

Instantiation is the act of creating an object from a class, allocating a dedicated region of memory for that object's own data; a constructor is a special method automatically run at that exact moment to set up its initial data.

A named piece of data belonging to a specific object — an instance attribute belongs to one object individually; a class attribute (static attribute) is shared identically across every object of that class.

A function that belongs specifically to a class, operating directly on a particular object's own attributes — an instance method operates on one object's data; a static method belongs to the class itself.
Calling another method directly on the exact result a previous method call just returned, in one single continuous expression, rather than writing each call out on its own separate line.
A mechanism letting one class (a subclass) be defined as an extension of another (a superclass), automatically receiving its attributes and methods while adding or overriding its own.
A subclass defining its own version of a method its superclass already defines — calling that method on a subclass object runs the subclass's own overriding version instead of the parent's original.

Code written to work with a general, parent-class type that, without modification, correctly works with any of its specific subclasses too, automatically calling whichever overridden method the real object actually has.

The OOP principle of keeping an object's internal data hidden or restricted from direct outside access, exposing only a specific, controlled set of methods through which other code is permitted to interact with it.

A keyword explicitly marking a given attribute or method as public (accessible from anywhere), private (accessible only within that same class), or protected (accessible to that class and its subclasses too).

A getter is a method whose entire job is returning a private attribute's current value in a controlled way; a setter's job is deliberately updating that value, typically after running validation logic first.

A function whose output depends only on its given input, with no reliance on external state and zero observable side effects on anything outside itself — the identical input always produces the identical output.

A pure function's most useful property: since a call always produces the identical result for the identical input, that call can be freely replaced anywhere by its own already-known result with zero change in behavior.

A function treated exactly like any other value — assignable to a variable, passable as an argument, returnable from another function; a higher-order function is one that accepts or returns another function.
A function passed into another function specifically to be called later, at some deliberately appropriate moment — a button's click handler is a classic, everyday example.
A function that retains real, genuine access to variables from the specific scope it was originally defined in, even after that surrounding scope has technically finished executing.
Software that tracks every change ever made to a project's files over time, letting you see exactly what changed, when, and by whom, and revert back to any previous known-working state.

A repository is a project tracked by Git along with its complete history; a commit is one deliberately saved snapshot within it; a branch is an independent, lightweight line of commits diverging from the main history.
Bringing one branch's accumulated changes back into another, combining both branches' separate histories together into one unified history going forward from that point.

What happens when Git attempts to merge two branches and discovers both modified the exact same lines of the same file in genuinely different, incompatible ways — requiring a human to manually resolve it.

A formal proposal to merge one branch's changes into another, typically opened through a hosting platform, displaying exactly what changed and inviting review before the merge is actually allowed to happen.
A copy of a repository hosted on a server accessible over the internet, that team members push their own completed commits up to and pull everyone else's completed commits down from.
The specific place where execution actually starts for the behavior you're trying to understand — a specific function being called, an event handler being triggered, or a script's very first line.
An agreed-upon, consistent style for naming variables, functions, and classes — snake_case separates words with underscores; camelCase joins words together, capitalizing each word after the first.

Surface-level conventions like indentation depth, spacing, and bracket placement, mechanically invisible to the machine running the code but a real lever for how quickly a human reader can parse its structure.
Code that's genuinely easy for a human to read, correctly understand, and safely modify later — explicitly not just code that happens to technically work correctly right now.

When a variable defined inside a narrower, inner scope shares the identical name as a different variable already defined in an outer scope, silently "hiding" the outer one for as long as the inner scope is active.

Programs built from large collections of hand-coded logical rules, written directly by human experts, meant to reproduce expert reasoning within one narrowly defined domain — transparent but brittle outside that domain.
A period of reduced research funding and public interest in AI, occurring when the field's practical results repeatedly fell short of its own earlier, often overhyped expectations.

A test proposed by Alan Turing asking whether a human evaluator, conversing by text with both a person and a machine, can reliably tell which is which — a behavioral standard, not a claim about internal awareness.

An active research area focused on developing methods for better understanding why a trained machine learning model produced one specific output rather than another, since its internal decision-making is hard to trace directly.

A model trained from data, the way any ML model is, whose learned structure — a sequence of individually readable yes/no questions branching to a final answer — remains genuinely traceable and human-inspectable afterward.

A neural network's individual, adjustable connection strengths (weights), organized into layers of simple computational units (neurons), each transforming values passed forward from the layer before it.

The training procedure comparing a network's output against the known-correct answer and using the size of that error to calculate how each individual weight should be nudged to make the next output slightly less wrong.
A network with many hidden layers stacked one after another — "deep" describes the number of layers, letting a network build up more abstract patterns out of simpler ones learned in earlier layers.
A simple nonlinear function applied to a neuron's weighted sum, letting a network represent complex, non-straight-line patterns rather than being limited to simple linear relationships.

Training is the extraordinarily compute-intensive process of adjusting a network's weights using example data; inference is the much cheaper process of using an already-trained, fixed-weight network to answer a new input.

A batch is a small group of training examples processed together for efficiency; an epoch is one complete pass through an entire training dataset, with large models commonly trained across multiple epochs.
A generation process where each new output token is produced based partly on the model's own previous outputs — meaning a model can't revise something it already generated earlier in a response.
The initial, enormous training run on a broad, general body of text, producing a general-purpose base model before any later fine-tuning narrows or adjusts its behavior for a specific purpose.
Few-shot prompting gives a model concrete examples of the desired output format; chain-of-thought prompting explicitly asks a model to show its reasoning step by step before giving a final answer.

Systematic patterns present in a model's training data — in how different groups of people are represented, for instance — that can be learned and reproduced in the model's own output, without anyone intending it.

Treating a model's answer as automatically authoritative rather than as one input to verify against other sources — a user who stops independently checking important output can end up worse off than one using a less capable tool skeptically.

The unit a language model actually operates over — often a whole word, sometimes a smaller fragment — produced by tokenization, the preprocessing step converting raw text into these numerical units before the model sees it.

The widely used algorithm behind how a model's fixed vocabulary gets built — starting from individual characters and repeatedly merging the most frequently co-occurring pair into a single new combined token.
The specific, fixed set of possible tokens a model can use, decided once and for all during training, typically containing tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand distinct entries.

The total number of a neural network's individual weights — a model described as "7B" or "70B" has that many billion parameters, a rough proxy for its raw capacity that also drives its memory and compute cost.

Reducing a model's memory footprint by storing each parameter using fewer bits than its original training precision, trading a small amount of precision for a large reduction in memory and compute needed to run it.
The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can consider at once within a single request — including the prompt, any provided documents, and the conversation's own prior responses.
The calculation letting a model weigh how relevant each other token in its current context is to understanding or predicting a given position, rather than processing text in one fixed, rigid order.

Continuing a model's training process further on top of an already pre-trained model, using a smaller curated dataset, permanently adjusting its weights toward a specific domain or style rather than just shaping one request.

A fine-tuning technique that adjusts a model's behavior using human ratings of which of several candidate responses is actually preferable — part of what turns a raw next-token predictor into a more helpful assistant.

A technique converting a piece of content into a list of numbers (a vector) constructed so that similar meaning produces similar, mathematically close vectors, even when the two pieces of text share no literal words.
A system purpose-built to efficiently find, among potentially millions of stored embedding vectors, the handful genuinely closest to a new query's own vector.
A standard mathematical calculation comparing the angle between two vectors, used to measure how close together, and therefore how similar in meaning, two embeddings actually are.

What happens when the most statistically fluent continuation a model generates simply isn't factually accurate — a direct structural consequence of being optimized for plausible text, not verified truth.

A setting controlling how much randomness a model's token selection involves — higher temperature increases variety and creativity but also the chance of a less reliably accurate continuation; lower temperature sticks closer to the model's most confident prediction.

A technique that searches a document collection for content relevant to a question, then inserts that retrieved material into a model's context window so it generates its answer grounded in real source material.

Breaking a long document into smaller, overlapping pieces before embedding and storing it, since a very long document embedded as one single vector tends to blur too many distinct topics together to match well.

A language model set up not just to produce a single block of text, but to actively take actions — calling tools, observing the results, and deciding what to do next — repeating this cycle toward a larger goal.

Following a pointer to actually read or modify the data it points at — dereferencing a pointer holding an invalid address is one of the most infamous categories of bug in low-level programming, often called a segmentation fault.

A value that, once created, can never be altered in place — any "modification" instead creates an entirely new value and leaves the original untouched, which is why an immutable value behaves safely even when many parts of a program hold the same reference to it.

A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem — the base case is the simple condition where it stops calling itself, and the recursive case is where it calls itself again while making genuine progress toward that base case.

A small block of memory pushed onto the call stack for each function call, holding its local variables and the spot to resume once it returns — a stack overflow happens when too many frames pile up, as with infinite or excessively deep recursion.
The tool computer science uses to describe how an algorithm's running time or memory use grows as its input size grows, ignoring constant factors and focusing purely on the dominant, long-run trend.

A single algorithm can have different Big O figures depending on the scenario described — Big O cited without qualification conventionally refers to the worst case, the guarantee that actually matters for real-world reliability.

Different systematic strategies for putting a collection into order: bubble and selection sort repeatedly scan and swap (O(n²)); insertion sort builds up a sorted portion one item at a time; merge sort and quicksort both use divide-and-conquer to reach O(n log n) on average.
terms.technical_term: Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Selection, Insertion, Merge, Quicksort)

terms.definition: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the original relative order of elements that compare as equal to each other — merge sort and insertion sort are typically stable; standard quicksort typically is not.

Linear search checks every element one at a time until it finds a match, working on any data at O(n); binary search repeatedly discards half the remaining range by comparing against the middle element, but requires the data already be sorted, running in O(log n).

An array of arrays, letting data be organized across two or more independent dimensions instead of just one — a jagged array is one whose inner arrays can have different lengths from each other, rather than forming a uniform, rectangular grid.
Joining two or more strings together into one longer string — because strings are immutable, every concatenation creates a brand-new string in memory rather than modifying the original one in place.

Deliberately converting a value from one data type to another — explicit casting is directly requested by the programmer; implicit casting (coercion) happens silently; widening casting loses no information, narrowing casting can silently discard some.

A special, distinct value meaning "there is intentionally no value here" — not the same as zero, an empty string, or false, and attempting to use it as though it held real data produces one of the most common runtime errors across virtually every mainstream language.

A compact, specialized pattern language for describing shapes of text rather than one exact literal string — metacharacters like \d, *, and + describe categories and repetition, and capture groups let a pattern extract just the matching portion it needs.

A marker on a specific line telling a debugger to pause execution right there so every variable currently in scope becomes directly inspectable — step over, step into, and step out are the three standard ways to resume once paused.

A data structure of nodes connected by edges, with exactly one root and no cycles, where every other node has exactly one parent — a binary tree restricts every node to at most two children, and a binary search tree additionally orders them so left is smaller and right is larger.

Systematic ways of visiting every node of a tree exactly once — in-order visits a binary search tree's nodes in fully sorted order; pre-order visits the current node before its subtrees; post-order visits both subtrees before the current node.

A graph is made of vertices (points) connected by edges — an undirected graph's edges work both ways, a directed graph's edges point one way only, and a weighted graph attaches a numeric cost to each edge.

An adjacency list has each vertex keep its own list of directly connected vertices, memory-efficient for sparse graphs; an adjacency matrix stores a full grid of every possible vertex pair, giving instant lookup at the cost of space proportional to the square of the vertex count.

A graph is connected if some path exists between every single pair of vertices, however roundabout; it's disconnected if at least one vertex or cluster has no path reaching some other vertex or cluster.

A priority queue always serves whichever item currently has the highest priority rather than strictly first-in-first-out; a heap is the tree-based structure almost universally used to implement it, guaranteeing the minimum (or maximum) value always sits at the root.

The process of restoring a heap's ordering property after insertion (sift-up, comparing a new item against its parent and swapping upward) or removal (sift-down, comparing the relocated root against its children and swapping downward).

An algorithmic paradigm that breaks a problem into smaller subproblems of the identical type, solves each independently (typically recursively), and combines their solutions into the answer for the original, larger problem.

BFS explores a graph level by level outward from a starting vertex using a queue, guaranteeing the shortest unweighted path; DFS follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking, using a stack or recursion.

The classic algorithm for finding the lowest-total-cost path between two vertices in a weighted graph, repeatedly selecting the unvisited vertex with the smallest known tentative distance and relaxing (updating) its neighbors' distances — correct only when no edge weight is negative.

An algorithmic technique for solving problems with overlapping subproblems by solving each distinct subproblem exactly once and storing its result — memoization caches results top-down through recursion, tabulation builds a table bottom-up through iteration.

A problem-solving approach that builds a solution step by step, always taking whichever choice looks locally best right now and never revisiting it — only produces the true optimal answer for problems that satisfy the greedy-choice property.

The degree to which one part of a program depends on and is entangled with another part's internal details — poor separation of concerns tends to produce tight coupling, while good separation tends to produce loose coupling.

Local state lives inside one function or component and disappears when it finishes; application state persists for as long as a program keeps running; persistent state survives even after the program stops, typically saved to a file or database.

An architectural pattern splitting an application into three separated roles: the Model (data and business rules), the View (presentation), and the Controller (handling input and coordinating between the other two).

A defined set of ways one program can request something from another without needing to know its internal implementation — a REST API organizes endpoints (a URL path plus an HTTP method) around resources, and versioning lets a changed API coexist safely alongside an older one.

Code that sits between an incoming request and the logic that ultimately handles it, running in a defined sequence and able to inspect, modify, respond to, or simply pass the request along to whatever comes next.

A try block holds code that might fail; a catch block runs if it does, rather than the program crashing outright — failing gracefully means providing a sensible fallback, failing loudly means letting an error be clearly reported.

Deliberately recording a program's significant events as it runs, organized by severity level (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR) so a developer can reconstruct what happened later — structured logging records events as machine-readable, labeled data rather than free-form text.

A small, automated, self-checking piece of code verifying that one function behaves correctly in isolation, following an arrange-act-assert shape — test coverage measures how much of a codebase is exercised by at least one test, and a regression is something that used to work but broke.

A named value that exists outside a program's source code, set differently in each environment (development, staging, production) it runs in, letting the exact same code run correctly and appropriately without ever needing secrets hardcoded directly into it.

A structured framework describing the phases a software project typically passes through — requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance — with the waterfall model running each phase to full completion strictly in order before the next begins.

Agile favors flexibility and continuous feedback over one rigid upfront plan; Scrum is its most common concrete framework, organizing work into fixed-length sprints pulled from a prioritized backlog, with daily stand-ups and roles like product owner and Scrum master.

A permissive license (like MIT) allows broad reuse with few conditions; a copyleft license (like the GPL) requires derivative works to be released under that same license; a proprietary license grants only narrow, tightly restricted permissions with no source code at all.

Designing and building software so people with disabilities can genuinely use it too — a screen reader reads on-screen content aloud, alt text is a descriptive text alternative for an image, and WCAG specifies concrete standards like minimum color contrast.
terms.technical_term: Accessibility (a11y) / Screen Reader / Alt Text / WCAG

terms.definition: A relational database organizes data into tables with a fixed, enforced schema and relates them through keys, queried with SQL; a non-relational (NoSQL) database doesn't require one rigid schema and organizes data using more flexible models instead.

A primary key is a column whose value uniquely identifies one row in a table; a foreign key is a column in one table referencing another table's primary key, establishing a relationship between them; a composite key combines two or more columns to be unique together.
terms.technical_term: Primary Key / Foreign Key / Composite Key

terms.definition: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four fundamental data operations, implemented in SQL by INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE.

An INNER JOIN returns only rows with a genuine match in both tables; a LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table regardless of a match, filling unmatched columns with null; a RIGHT JOIN reverses that; a junction table connects two tables in a many-to-many relationship.

An auxiliary structure built on one or more columns that dramatically speeds up lookups against them, typically implemented as a B-tree giving O(log n) lookups instead of a full O(n) table scan, at the cost of extra storage and somewhat slower writes.

A group of database operations treated as a single, indivisible unit. ACID is the formal set of guarantees a well-implemented transaction provides — atomicity means all-or-nothing, and durability means a committed change survives even a crash afterward.

The disciplined process of organizing a relational database's tables to eliminate redundant data duplication through a sequence of rules (1NF, 2NF, 3NF); denormalization is the deliberate opposite, reintroducing controlled redundancy for better read performance.

Document databases store flexible, JSON-like nested records; key-value stores map a unique key straight to a value for extremely fast lookup; column-family databases organize by column for large-scale analytical reads; graph databases store vertices and edges directly.

In a distributed database spread across several machines, you can only fully guarantee two of three properties at once: consistency (every node sees the same data at the same time), availability (every request gets a response), and partition tolerance (the system keeps working despite network disruption).

The declared action of an HTTP request — GET retrieves without changing anything, POST creates something new, PUT replaces a resource entirely, PATCH partially updates it, DELETE removes it. Idempotency is whether repeating the exact same request produces the same net effect as doing it once.

A short, standardized three-digit number attached to every HTTP response communicating its general outcome — 2xx means success, 4xx means the client's request itself was the problem, and 5xx means something went wrong on the server's own side.

A key-value pair sent alongside an HTTP request or response, separate from the actual body, describing something about the message, its sender, or how it should be handled — content negotiation lets a client's Accept header request a preferred response format.

A small piece of data a server sends to a browser, which the browser automatically resends on later requests — typically holding a session ID pointing to a server-side session record, since HTTP itself has no built-in memory between separate requests.

Authentication verifies who someone actually is; authorization, which always depends on authentication having already happened, determines what that identified person is actually allowed to do — role-based access control (RBAC) assigns permissions by role rather than per user.

A browser-enforced mechanism governing when JavaScript on one origin is allowed to read the response of a request made to a different origin — the same-origin policy is the default restriction, and a preflight OPTIONS request checks permission first for more sensitive cross-origin requests.

Deciding when a cached value has become stale and needs refreshing — widely considered one of the hardest problems in computer science, commonly handled with a time-to-live (TTL) after which a value automatically expires; a CDN caches content geographically close to users.

Concurrency is a program's logical structure supporting multiple overlapping in-progress tasks; parallelism specifically means multiple tasks physically executing at the exact same instant, typically on separate CPU cores — a single core can be concurrent without ever being parallel.

A syntax letting code pause at an await point to wait for a slow operation without blocking the rest of the program, while still reading top-to-bottom like ordinary sequential code — a promise (or future) is the value an async operation returns immediately, to be resolved or rejected later.

A technique restricting how many requests a client can make within a defined time window to protect a system from being overwhelmed — the token bucket algorithm allows brief bursts while enforcing a long-term average rate; fixed and sliding window are two other common implementations.

How an OS scheduler decides which process runs next — round-robin gives each process an equal time slice; priority scheduling runs higher-priority processes first but risks starvation, where a low-priority process waits indefinitely.

Each process gets its own private virtual address space, with the OS and a memory management unit (MMU) translating every virtual address into wherever it truly lives in physical RAM — paging divides memory into fixed-size pages, and a page fault occurs when a needed page is on disk instead of RAM.

A mutex is a lock exactly one thread can hold at a time, protecting a critical section of code that touches shared data; a semaphore generalizes this to allow up to some defined number of threads through simultaneously.

Two or more threads each waiting on a resource the other currently holds, so neither can ever proceed — occurs specifically when mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait all hold simultaneously; prevented in practice by a consistent, fixed lock-ordering convention.

A human-readable, symbolic representation of raw machine code, using short mnemonics like MOV and ADD in place of binary patterns, with each instruction corresponding one-to-one to a real machine instruction — a CPU register is a tiny, extremely fast storage location built into the chip itself.

RISC favors a smaller set of simple, uniform instructions well suited to pipelining; CISC offers a larger set of more complex instructions that can accomplish more per instruction — pipelining overlaps a CPU's fetch, decode, and execute stages across several instructions at once to improve throughput.

An LLM API sending its response back incrementally, token by token, as it's actually being generated, rather than making the caller wait for the entire response to finish before receiving anything at all back.

The system prompt sets a model's overall role, behavior, and constraints for an entire conversation; the user prompt is the specific request made in one moment. Prompt injection is when a crafted user prompt attempts to override the system prompt's own intended instructions.
terms.technical_term: System Prompt vs. User Prompt / Prompt Injection

terms.definition: Constraining a language model to reliably return data in a specific, predictable, machine-readable format like JSON instead of free-form prose, so surrounding application code can parse it directly without fragile text-parsing logic.

Breaking one large, complex task into several smaller prompts run in a defined sequence, where each step's output becomes the next step's input — applying the same divide-and-conquer strategy used in ordinary code, but to prompts instead.

The family of specialized indexing algorithms vector databases use to find the closest stored vectors to a query vector quickly at large scale, trading a small, bounded amount of exactness for dramatically faster search speed than comparing against every stored vector one at a time.

Deliberately sending simpler, lower-stakes requests to a smaller, cheaper, faster model while reserving a larger, more expensive, more capable model specifically for requests that are genuinely more complex or carry higher real stakes if something goes wrong.

Describing an AI coding assistant writing real, working code from a natural-language description, with a human largely guiding it through general intent rather than typing every line themselves — the generated code still runs through every ordinary mechanism of compilation, execution, and testing.

A named, proven, reusable solution to a commonly recurring software design problem — not finished code to copy, but a general template experienced engineers have already worked out, tested, and given a shared name.

A pattern ensuring a class has exactly one instance throughout a program's lifetime, with one well-defined access point every part of the program uses to reach it — lazy initialization delays actually creating that instance until it's genuinely first requested.

A pattern centralizing object creation logic into one dedicated function or class rather than scattering construction steps throughout a codebase — an abstract factory extends this to produce an entire family of related objects meant to work together consistently.

A pattern letting one object (the subject) automatically notify a list of registered observers whenever its own state changes, without needing to know anything specific about them — publish-subscribe applies the same idea across an entire distributed system.

MVVM lets a View automatically observe and re-render from a ViewModel's state; MVP instead has a Presenter explicitly, manually update the View; Flux/Redux route every state change through one single, centralized, traceable store instead.

A commonly repeated approach that looks reasonable but reliably causes real problems — a God object takes on too many responsibilities, spaghetti code has no traceable structure, and over-engineering solves problems a project doesn't actually have; refactoring is the remedy once one is recognized.

Vertical scaling means making one machine more powerful, simple but with a hard ceiling; horizontal scaling means adding more machines and distributing work across them, essentially unlimited but far more complex to coordinate. Elasticity means a system also scales back down automatically once demand subsides.

The specific part of a system that's actually constraining its overall performance — adding capacity anywhere else provides little real improvement, which is why identifying the genuine bottleneck before scaling anything is the practical starting point.

A component sitting in front of multiple servers and distributing incoming requests across them — least-connections routes to whichever server has the fewest active connections, sticky sessions keep one user's requests on one server, and health checks stop routing to servers that fail to respond.

Cache-aside has the application check the cache first and populate it on a miss; write-through automatically writes to the cache the instant the database is written. An eviction policy like LRU (least-recently-used) decides which entry to discard once a cache is full.

A server in a CDN's globally distributed network, physically positioned close to actual end users so requests don't have to travel all the way to one distant origin server — edge computing extends this by running genuine application logic on those same distributed servers, not just caching static files.

A monolith builds an entire application as one unified codebase deployed as one unit, simple but increasingly unwieldy as it grows; microservices split an application into many small, independently deployable services communicating over network APIs, more flexible but with real added coordination cost.

A mechanism letting one part of a system place a message for another part to process whenever it's ready, decoupling their exact timing — a dead-letter queue catches messages that repeatedly fail processing rather than retrying forever or discarding them silently.

XSS happens when unescaped user input is displayed on a page and executes as code in other users' browsers; stored XSS persists the attack in a database so it affects every future visitor. CSRF instead tricks a victim's browser into unknowingly submitting a genuine request using their own valid session.

Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt, fast but requiring a securely shared key beforehand; asymmetric encryption uses a linked public/private key pair, solving that key-sharing problem. A digital signature uses the same key pair to prove a message's authenticity rather than to keep it secret.
terms.technical_term: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Encryption / Digital Signature

terms.definition: Encryption in transit protects data while it's actively traveling across a network, like HTTPS; encryption at rest protects data while it's sitting stored on a disk or in a database — a system can be protected by one without the other, and a fully secure system needs both.
terms.technical_term: Encryption in Transit vs. at Rest

terms.definition: Adding a small amount of random, unique data to each password before hashing it, so identical passwords produce different stored hashes and defeat a rainbow table (a precomputed table mapping common passwords to their hashes). Key stretching applies the hash function many thousands of times to further slow brute-force guessing.

Transport Layer Security encrypts data traveling between a browser and server and verifies the server's identity through a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority — without that verification, a man-in-the-middle attacker could impersonate the real server even over an encrypted connection.

Any user, process, or component should be granted only the minimum access genuinely necessary to do its job — privilege creep is the gradual failure mode where accumulated permissions from past roles never get revoked when they're no longer needed.
terms.technical_term: Principle of Least Privilege / Privilege Creep

terms.definition: Dedicated systems that store secrets encrypted at rest, tightly control who can retrieve them, and support key rotation — regularly replacing a secret on a schedule to limit how long a leaked one stays useful. Secret sprawl is losing track of how many secrets exist and who has access to them as an organization grows.
terms.technical_term: Secrets Management / Key Rotation / Secret Sprawl

terms.definition: A tool that measures where a running program actually spends its time and memory, function by function — a sampling profiler periodically checks what's currently executing with low overhead; an instrumenting profiler tracks every call precisely but can slow the program down. A flame graph visualizes the results by function width.

Spending significant effort optimizing code before measurement has actually shown it's a genuine bottleneck — micro-optimization is the narrower case of shaving negligible time off an expression that runs too rarely for the improvement to matter at all.

Calculating results ahead of time, proactively, before anyone requests them, rather than on demand — cache warming precomputes a cache's most likely-needed entries in advance; a materialized view stores an expensive query's result as an actual table, refreshed on a schedule.

The specific, actual sequence of internal steps a database engine takes to fulfill a query, revealing whether it's genuinely using an available index or silently falling back to a slower full table scan — invisible from the SQL text alone.

Accidentally running one separate database query per item inside a loop instead of one combined query for everything — connection pooling reuses a small set of already-open connections instead of opening a new one per query; eager loading explicitly fetches related data upfront to avoid the trap.
terms.technical_term: N+1 Query Problem / Connection Pooling / Eager Loading

terms.definition: A lock coordinated across multiple separate machines over a network rather than within one machine's memory. Optimistic concurrency control instead skips locking entirely, checking right before writing whether the underlying data changed since it was read, and retrying only if a genuine conflict occurred.

Rather than guaranteeing every machine sees a perfectly synchronized view of shared data at every instant, many distributed systems accept a brief, bounded window of disagreement, trusting it will resolve and converge shortly afterward, in exchange for better performance and availability.

A set of practices and a cultural approach closing the gap between writing code and reliably running it in production through shared responsibility and automation. SRE applies a more explicit, quantitative version of the same goals; a blameless postmortem reviews an incident to find systemic fixes, not to assign individual blame.

Continuous Integration automatically builds and tests code on every change; Continuous Deployment/Delivery automatically ships passing code to production.
