A rollback reverts to the last working version; canary and blue-green deployments both reduce release risk by rolling changes out gradually or via an instant switch-back.

A packaged, portable unit bundling an application with everything it needs to run identically anywhere — a Docker image is the reusable blueprint, a Dockerfile defines how it's built, and container orchestration (like Kubernetes) manages running many containers across a fleet of machines.

A virtual machine is a rentable slice of a physical server behaving like an independent computer; serverless runs code on demand without the customer managing any server at all. An availability zone is a physically distinct part of a cloud region; vendor lock-in is the cost of depending too heavily on one provider's specific services.

Defining server, database, and network setup in version-controlled configuration files rather than manual dashboard clicks — declarative configuration describes the desired end state rather than the steps to reach it, directly preventing configuration drift, where a live system's real setup silently diverges from what anyone intended.
terms.technical_term: Infrastructure as Code / Declarative Configuration / Configuration Drift

terms.definition: Monitoring continuously tracks a running system's health in real time; alerting automatically notifies the right people when something goes wrong. Alert fatigue is when too-frequent alerts train people to ignore them; distributed tracing reconstructs one request's full journey across many microservices; p99 is the response time experienced by the slowest 1% of requests.

A structured, standardized test measuring how well an AI model performs on a specific task against known-correct answers. Benchmark contamination happens when a model's training data included the eval's own questions; LLM-as-judge uses a separate model to judge open-ended qualities a fixed answer can't capture.

Several distinct AI agents, each specialized for a sub-task, coordinating toward one larger goal with real autonomy over their own next steps — agent orchestration is the coordinating mechanism deciding which agent acts next and when the overall task is complete.

Combining vector-embedding-based semantic search with traditional keyword search, since semantic search alone can underweight exact keywords or unusual proper nouns. Re-ranking uses a separate specialized model to judge retrieved results' relevance more precisely than raw similarity alone.

Research into making capable AI systems reliably do what humans actually intend, not just technically satisfy their literal instructions. Reward hacking is exploiting a measurable proxy without achieving the real goal; interpretability studies a model's internal reasoning; corrigibility is remaining willing to be corrected or shut down.
terms.technical_term: AI Alignment / Reward Hacking / Interpretability / Corrigibility

terms.definition: Keeping a human actively approving high-stakes AI decisions before they take effect (human in the loop) rather than merely monitoring after the fact (human on the loop). Red-teaming deliberately tries to break a system before real attackers do; graceful degradation is a deliberate fallback plan for when an AI component fails or is unavailable.
terms.technical_term: Human in the Loop / Red-Teaming / Graceful Degradation

terms.definition: Python's own official design philosophy, shipped inside the language itself as a runnable poem (type `import this`) — its most quoted line, "explicit is better than implicit," favors code that shows its own behavior directly over relying on hidden, invisible steps.

A dict comprehension (`{k: v for k, v in pairs}`) builds a dictionary; a set comprehension (`{x for x in items}`) builds a set; a generator expression (`(x*2 for x in numbers)`) produces values lazily one at a time instead of building the whole collection upfront — all four share the same `for ... if ...` structure as a list comprehension.

A function that produces a sequence of values lazily, one at a time, using `yield` instead of `return` — `yield` pauses the function's execution, hands back one value, and remembers exactly where it stopped, ready to resume the next time a value is requested.

A function that wraps another function, adding behavior before and/or after it runs without touching the original function's own code, applied with `@decorator_name` syntax — `functools.wraps` is the standard fix for a decorated function otherwise losing its original name and docstring.

An object guaranteeing setup code runs before a block begins and cleanup code runs after it ends, whether the block finished normally or crashed — implemented through `__enter__` (setup) and `__exit__` (cleanup), used with Python's `with` statement.

An isolated Python installation created for one specific project, with its own separate set of installed packages kept apart from any other project's packages, even on the same machine — solving the problem of two projects needing incompatible versions of the same library.

Python's standard package manager, installing libraries from PyPI. A requirements.txt file lists a project's exact dependencies, often pinned to specific versions, so anyone installing from it reliably recreates the same setup — pyproject.toml is the newer, more structured file increasingly replacing it.

An array holding one single, fixed data type stored contiguously in memory, letting NumPy perform a mathematical operation across an entire array at once in optimized compiled code — vectorization is writing an operation like `array * 2` to run across every element at once instead of looping.

A pandas structure conceptually similar to a spreadsheet, with labeled rows and named columns, built on top of NumPy arrays — letting a column be referenced by a meaningful name and filtered, grouped, or cleaned in a single readable line rather than manual loop-based bookkeeping.

Streamlit re-runs an entire script from top to bottom on every single user interaction, so an ordinary variable resets on every click — st.session_state is the special, persistent storage mechanism that deliberately survives across these full-script reruns.

Flask is a minimal, deliberately flexible Python web framework providing only the genuine essentials; Django is a considerably larger, more opinionated framework shipping a built-in admin panel, ORM, and authentication system ready to use out of the box.

A layer letting a developer interact with a relational database using ordinary objects and method calls rather than writing raw SQL query strings by hand — Django ships its own built-in ORM; SQLAlchemy provides the same capability independently of any particular framework.

An optional annotation on a function's signature stating its expected argument and return types — not enforced by Python's interpreter at runtime at all; a static type checker like mypy is a separate tool that reads and checks these hints without ever running the code.

aliases: easier to ask forgiveness than permission
terms.definition: EAFP means attempting an operation and handling the exception if it fails, Python's generally preferred style; LBYL means checking every precondition first. EAFP avoids a TOCTOU bug (time-of-check to time-of-use), where the checked state could change before the action actually runs.

A coroutine is a function that can be paused and resumed, defined with `async def`, run by asyncio's event loop. The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) prevents multiple threads from executing Python bytecode at the exact same instant even on a multi-core machine, which is why CPU-bound parallelism in Python needs `multiprocessing` instead of plain threading.

Programmatically extracting specific data out of a webpage's raw HTML content rather than a human manually reading and copying it out by hand — BeautifulSoup handles simpler, smaller-scale scraping; Scrapy is a fuller framework for large-scale, many-page crawling.

A project convention placing the actual application package inside a dedicated src/ folder rather than at the project's top level, preventing Python from accidentally importing a local in-development copy instead of the properly installed one — __init__.py's presence is what historically marked a folder as an importable package.

Modern JavaScript's `let`/`const` confine a variable to the exact block it's declared in, unlike the older `var`, which is visible throughout its entire enclosing function. Hoisting is a declaration being conceptually moved to the top of its scope before code runs; the temporal dead zone is the window where a block-scoped variable exists but can't yet be referenced.
terms.technical_term: Block Scoping (let/const) / Hoisting / Temporal Dead Zone

terms.definition: A Promise moves through exactly one of three states in one direction only — pending, fulfilled (settled successfully), or rejected (settled with an error) — with `.then()`/`.catch()` attaching what happens once it settles. Callback hell is the deeply nested, hard-to-follow chain of callbacks Promises and async/await both exist to replace.

Promise.all() runs multiple async operations concurrently and resolves once every one has completed; Promise.race() settles as soon as the first one does; Promise.allSettled() waits for every Promise regardless of whether each individually succeeded or failed.

The standard, modern tools for locating specific elements within the DOM tree, accepting a CSS selector string and returning the matching element or elements — the everyday starting point for locating an element before reading or modifying it.

A webpage that never performs a traditional full reload after its initial load, instead fetching data asynchronously and updating itself continuously through DOM manipulation — each DOM change can trigger the browser to recalculate layout (reflow) and repaint the affected pixels, a real, measurable cost of doing many small updates instead of batching them.

JavaScript's event loop maintains two separate queues — a microtask queue where Promise callbacks go, and a macrotask queue where setTimeout callbacks go — always fully draining the microtask queue before picking up the next single macrotask, which is exactly why a Promise's `.then()` reliably runs before a `setTimeout(callback, 0)` does.

A genuinely separate thread JavaScript specifically provides for offloading long-running computational work, running independently of the single main thread and communicating back to it through explicit message-passing rather than shared memory.

React and Vue compute an in-memory representation of what the updated UI should look like, compare it against what's currently displayed, and apply only the minimal set of real DOM changes needed — this comparison-and-update process is reconciliation. JSX blends HTML-like markup directly inside JavaScript code; props are the inputs a component accepts from whatever component uses it.

npm's manifest file listing a project's dependencies, scripts, and metadata; package-lock.json records the exact, precise version of every package actually installed, including every indirect dependency, guaranteeing the same dependency tree gets reproduced on any machine.

A tool that scans a project's full dependency tree, including every indirect dependency, against a database of known security vulnerabilities and reports any it finds, often alongside a suggested fix.

What `this` refers to inside a JavaScript function depends on how that function was called, not where it was defined — an arrow function instead has no binding of its own and inherits `this` lexically from its surrounding scope at the point it was written, which is why arrow functions became the preferred default for callbacks. `.bind()` explicitly locks a function's `this` regardless of how it's later invoked.
terms.technical_term: this Binding / Lexical this / Arrow Function

terms.definition: JSON.parse() converts a JSON-formatted text string into a usable JavaScript object; JSON.stringify() performs the reverse, converting a JavaScript object into a JSON-formatted string — JavaScript's own built-in implementation of the general serialization/deserialization concept, requiring no separate library.

V8 is the JavaScript engine Chrome's browser uses, embedded by Node.js into a standalone program with no browser or DOM wrapped around it. Full-stack JavaScript means building an entire application's frontend and backend both in the same language.

A superset of JavaScript adding static types that are actually enforced at compile time, catching a mismatch before code ever runs — unlike Python's unenforced type hints. Type erasure means the type information is entirely gone from the compiled JavaScript output; the `any` type is a deliberate escape hatch that opts a specific value back out of type checking.

A runtime safety check the JVM performs automatically — accessing an array index outside its valid range in Java throws a specific, catchable exception rather than silently reading whatever unrelated memory happens to sit at that invalid location, the class of bug (a buffer overrun) that has caused serious security vulnerabilities in languages without this protection.

Writing `List<String>` rather than a plain, unparameterized `List` lets the compiler verify only strings are ever added to or retrieved from that specific list, catching a mismatched insertion at compile time rather than allowing it to silently succeed and only fail later when the misplaced value is read back out.

A Java feature automatically generating the constructor, field accessors, and several other standard methods a hand-written class holding a fixed set of data would otherwise require spelling out line by line — still an ordinary class underneath, just one the compiler generates most of the repetitive parts of automatically.

A contract specifying which public methods a class must implement, without dictating how — enforced by the compiler, unlike an informal convention. An abstract class can provide some actual implemented behavior and a class extends only one; a class can implement multiple interfaces at once. A functional interface declares exactly one abstract method and can be implemented inline with a lambda.
terms.technical_term: Java Interface / Abstract Class / Functional Interface

terms.definition: An exception (like NullPointerException) representing a genuine programming bug rather than a foreseeable, recoverable condition — Java's compiler doesn't force code to catch or declare it, unlike a checked exception. Every exception type sits somewhere in a single hierarchy rooted at Throwable, which splits into Error and Exception, with RuntimeException and its subclasses forming the unchecked branch.

Collections Framework implementations keeping their entries in sorted order at all times, backed internally by a self-balancing binary search tree rather than a hash table — trading HashMap/HashSet's raw average-case speed for the ability to efficiently retrieve entries in sorted order.

The dominant framework for building Java web applications, handling routing, database connections, and dependency injection automatically. Dependency injection is a pattern where a component's required dependencies are automatically supplied by the framework rather than the component constructing them itself. Spring Boot layers sensible default configuration on top of the broader framework.
terms.technical_term: Spring Framework / Spring Boot / Dependency Injection

terms.definition: Modern Android compiles Java bytecode ahead of time into native machine code specific to the device's processor through the Android Runtime (ART), rather than running a standard JVM — an Activity represents one screen, a Service represents background work, and a BroadcastReceiver responds to system-wide events, each following Android's own component lifecycle rules.

Most modern JVM garbage collectors trace reachability from a fixed set of roots rather than counting references, correctly reclaiming even mutually-referencing objects nothing else can reach. A stop-the-world pause briefly halts other work to safely identify unreferenced memory; generational collection (like G1) collects short-lived young objects far more frequently and cheaply than longer-lived ones.
terms.technical_term: Reachability Tracing / Stop-the-World Pause / Generational GC

terms.definition: Java's two dominant build tools, handling dependency download, compilation, testing, and packaging into a distributable JAR file. Maven uses a rigid, declarative XML configuration (pom.xml); Gradle uses a more flexible, programmatic build script (build.gradle) written in Groovy or Kotlin.

C#'s structural parallel to Java's bytecode — source code compiles into this hardware-independent intermediate form, run by the CLR, rather than directly into native machine code. The Base Class Library (BCL) is .NET's own standard library, providing ready-made functionality shared across every .NET language.

A deliberate shorthand for a property needing no custom logic, automatically generating a hidden backing field and standard get/set accessors — an init-only property can be set only during an object's initial construction, then permanently locked against further modification.

Most LINQ queries don't actually run the moment they're written — only when their results are genuinely iterated over or a method forcing immediate evaluation is called. Query syntax reads like SQL; method syntax chains methods directly. IQueryable<T> lets the same query syntax get translated into an entirely different query language, like SQL, rather than running directly in memory.
terms.technical_term: Deferred Execution / Query Syntax vs. Method Syntax

terms.definition: C#'s own equivalent of a JavaScript Promise or Python asyncio coroutine — represents an operation that will complete at some future point, either successfully with a result or with an exception. An async method compiles into a state machine the .NET runtime manages; ConfigureAwait(false) opts a library out of resuming on one specific designated thread after an await.

Unity's basic building block, representing anything present in a game's world, with C# scripts attached to define its behavior — Start() runs once when a GameObject first becomes active, Update() runs once per rendered frame. A Unity coroutine uses yield return to spread logic across multiple frames, scheduled by Unity's frame loop rather than an event loop waiting on I/O.

A value type in C# — assigning or passing it copies its actual data, producing independent copies, unlike a class, which is a reference type. Boxing wraps a value type inside a heap-allocated object so it can be handled through a reference; unboxing reverses that process; the ref keyword lets a struct be passed by reference to avoid repeated copying.

A C# variant combining a record's convenient, boilerplate-reduced syntax with genuine value-type, struct-style copy semantics — distinct from a plain record class, which remains a reference type despite its similarly reduced boilerplate.

The compiler technique behind C#'s nullable reference type warnings: tracking, path by path through a method's code, whether a nullable variable has actually been checked for null before it's used, and only suppressing the warning once it can genuinely verify a null value can't reach that point unhandled. Tony Hoare, who introduced the null reference, later called it his own "billion-dollar mistake."

Microsoft's primary framework for building C# web applications, playing the same comprehensive, batteries-included role Django and Spring play for Python and Java. Entity Framework is C#'s ORM, translating LINQ queries into real SQL; Minimal APIs let a full working route be defined in a single line without the framework's more traditional controller-class structure.
terms.technical_term: ASP.NET Core / Entity Framework / Minimal APIs

terms.definition: C# and .NET's own package manager, occupying the same role pip and npm play for Python and JavaScript. A project's dependencies are declared in its .csproj file; Central Package Management lets every project in a larger solution share one centrally declared set of package versions rather than each pinning its own, potentially inconsistently.

The full IDE Microsoft builds specifically for deep, integrated C# and .NET support — genuinely different from the considerably lighter, general-purpose Visual Studio Code editor despite the similar name. IntelliSense is Microsoft's name for its smart, context-aware autocomplete, relying directly on the compiler's own live, certain knowledge of every variable's exact type.
terms.technical_term: Visual Studio / Visual Studio Code / IntelliSense

terms.definition: C++'s manual allocation keywords — new requests a block of heap memory and returns a pointer to it; delete explicitly releases that block back to the system. A dangling pointer (use-after-free) is using a pointer after its memory has already been freed; a double-free is calling delete twice on the same pointer, corrupting the heap's own bookkeeping.

Incrementing or decrementing a pointer directly to move it to the next or previous element in a contiguous block of memory — a powerful, low-level capability with no real equivalent in most memory-safe languages. Pass-by-value copies an argument entirely; pass-by-reference and pass-by-pointer both give a function access to the original without copying. const correctness lets the compiler enforce a promise not to modify data through a given reference or pointer.
terms.technical_term: Pointer Arithmetic / Pass-by-Value / Pass-by-Reference / const Correctness

terms.definition: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization — tying a resource's entire lifetime directly to an object's own lifetime, acquired in its constructor and automatically released in its destructor. Stack unwinding is the guaranteed process of calling every local object's destructor, in reverse order of construction, as an exception propagates up through the call stack.
terms.technical_term: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) / Stack Unwinding

terms.definition: The Standard Template Library — C++'s own standard, highly optimized, ready-made implementations of common data structures and algorithms, written generically using templates so the same implementation works with any type at zero runtime cost. An iterator is the shared interface letting STL algorithms work across genuinely different underlying container types.

A single function or class written once that works generically across many types — template instantiation is the compiler generating a fully specialized, concrete compiled version for each distinct type combination actually used, entirely at compile time. Code bloat is the resulting increase in final executable size from generating a separate version per type; template specialization lets a developer override the generic behavior for one specific type.
terms.technical_term: C++ Template / Template Instantiation / Code Bloat

terms.definition: unique_ptr represents sole, exclusive ownership of dynamically allocated memory, enforced at compile time; shared_ptr allows multiple owners through an internal reference count, freeing the memory only once that count drops to zero; weak_ptr is a non-owning reference that doesn't itself contribute to the count, specifically to break reference cycles shared_ptr alone can't resolve.

C++ compilation's three sequential stages: preprocessing performs pure text substitution (like #include), compiling translates each source file independently into object code, and linking combines those object files into one executable, resolving cross-file references. A linker error means an implementation was never found anywhere in the combined program; a header guard prevents a header's contents from being inserted more than once into the same file.
terms.technical_term: Preprocessing / Linking / Linker Error / Header Guard

terms.definition: Storing data contiguously in memory (as STL containers like vector do) so a CPU's memory cache can load and reuse many consecutive elements efficiently in a tight, repeated loop — a real, measurable performance concern in game-engine code. Unreal Engine is built entirely in C++ and exposes it directly to developers; Blueprint is its visual scripting layer built on top of that C++ core.

An operation the C++ standard deliberately places no requirement on — a compiler is fully permitted to do anything at all, including producing correct-looking results on one machine and silently wrong ones on another. Implementation-defined behavior instead requires each compiler to pick one consistent, documented behavior and stick to it; a sanitizer instruments a program specifically to detect likely undefined-behavior patterns during testing.

The dominant tool for managing C++ project builds across different platforms and compilers — it doesn't compile code itself, instead generating the platform-appropriate build instructions for whatever underlying build system is installed. CMakeLists.txt is its own configuration file; vcpkg and Conan are two competing package managers addressing C++'s historically fragmented dependency-management landscape.

The precise, strict meaning of the "C" in the CAP theorem — the guarantee that any read, from any machine, reflects the most recent completed write, as if there were really only one copy of the data being read and written in a strict, ordered sequence, a much stronger guarantee than the everyday sense of "the data is basically fine."

The majority threshold a distributed consensus system requires before treating a proposal as accepted — since two different majorities among the same group can never both exist simultaneously, a confirmed quorum decision is permanently safe. Raft and Paxos are the two best-known majority-voting consensus algorithms; Raft breaks the process into leader election, log replication, and safety.

A conflict-free replicated data type — a data structure engineered so that merging concurrent updates, in any order, always produces the same final result on every replica, with no explicit conflict-resolution logic needed. A gossip protocol spreads updates by having each machine periodically share what it knows with a few random neighbors; last write wins resolves conflicts by keeping whichever update carries the latest timestamp.
terms.technical_term: CRDT (Conflict-Free Replicated Data Type) / Gossip Protocol

terms.definition: The chosen field used to decide which shard a given piece of data belongs on — a poorly chosen shard key produces a hot shard, where one shard ends up holding a disproportionate share of the data and traffic. Resharding is redistributing data across a different number of shards as a dataset grows, one of the more operationally difficult tasks in running a large-scale system.

In synchronous replication, a write isn't confirmed until a replica (or a majority) has stored it, guaranteeing durability at the cost of latency; in asynchronous replication, the write is confirmed immediately and copied to replicas afterward, faster but with a real window where a failure can lose it. A primary-replica (leader-follower) setup has one designated machine accept all writes.

The mechanism letting every token in a transformer's input look directly at every other token in one step, computed by transforming each token into a query (what it's looking for), a key (what it offers), and a value, then blending values together weighted by how relevant each token's key is to the current query.

An empirical relationship describing how a language model's performance improves, in a smooth, predictable, power-law way, as model size, training data, and compute all grow together — DeepMind's 2022 Chinchilla paper found model size and training data should scale together in proportion, correcting an earlier, expensive over-investment in size alone.

Removing near-identical repeated content from a training corpus so a model doesn't over-memorize it; quality filtering scores and discards poorly-written text; safety filtering removes clearly harmful content; data mixing deliberately decides what proportion of the final training set comes from which source.

A model trained on human comparative judgments (a preference dataset) to predict how highly a human would rate a given response, used to further train a language model through reinforcement learning. Direct preference optimization (DPO) achieves a similar result without training a separate reward model or running the full reinforcement learning loop.

Storing a transformer's already-computed keys and values from each previous token so generating the next token only requires new computation for that one token. Batching processes many requests together to share the cost of loading model parameters into memory; distillation trains a smaller "student" model to imitate a larger "teacher" model's outputs.

A deliberately simple abstract model of computation — an infinite tape, a read-write head, and a finite table of rules — that can, in principle, perform any computation any computer of any design ever will be able to perform. The Church-Turing thesis claims anything intuitively computable can be computed by one; Turing completeness is the formal property of being exactly as powerful as a Turing machine.
terms.technical_term: Turing Machine / Church-Turing Thesis / Turing Completeness

terms.definition: The proof technique behind the halting problem's impossibility result — assuming a universal halting-decider exists, then constructing a program that does the opposite of whatever that decider predicts about itself, producing a genuine contradiction no matter what the decider answers.

A problem is NP-complete if it's in NP and every other problem in NP can be reduced into it using only polynomial extra work — meaning a fast algorithm for even one NP-complete problem would prove P equals NP for all of them. The boolean satisfiability problem was the first proven NP-complete.

A substantial, self-directed piece of work, built without a tutorial dictating every step, that demonstrates the accumulated skills of everything learned up to this point — chosen and shaped by the learner rather than assigned wholesale by someone else.

A label many open-source projects use to flag problems that are genuinely real and useful but deliberately scoped small enough not to require deep, months-long codebase familiarity — a curated entry point for newcomers. Issue triaging means confirming whether a reported bug is genuinely real and reproducible.

An unordered collection that never allows duplicate values — attempting to add a value already present simply does nothing, leaving the set unchanged — built specifically to make checking whether a value already exists dramatically faster than scanning through an array one item at a time.

The input text a person provides to a language model. Since a model has no memory outside of whatever text is actually present in its current context window, each request is effectively self-contained — meaning how a prompt is phrased directly and measurably shapes the quality of what comes back.

A data structure made of vertices (points, or nodes) connected by edges, with no restriction on how those connections loop, cross, or multiply — considerably more flexible and general than a tree, and capable of representing any network of relationships at all, like a subway map or a social network.

A server-side record that persists information about one visitor across multiple separate requests — since HTTP itself has no built-in memory between requests, a session is what actually lets a website recognize the same visitor as they click from page to page. A cookie is simply the mechanism carrying that session's ID back and forth.

The act of an operating system pausing one running process, saving exactly enough of its state to resume it later, and loading a different process's saved state in its place — the actual mechanism underneath process scheduling that makes a single CPU core look like it's running many programs at once.

The layered arrangement of increasingly larger, increasingly slower memory a CPU checks in order before finally falling back to RAM — a small, extremely fast cache sits closest to the CPU, backed by a larger, slightly slower one, and so on — so the common case of reusing recently-touched data stays fast without requiring every memory access to be that fast.

An attack where user-provided input is inserted directly into a database query without being safely escaped or separated from the query's actual structural syntax first — letting an attacker craft input that changes what the query itself means, rather than being treated as a plain value the query is merely searching for. A parameterized query, which keeps input and query structure strictly separate, is the standard defense.

A procedure letting multiple independent machines, none of which fully trusts the others' current state, agree on a single value or sequence of events even when some machines are slow, crash, or send conflicting information. The general problem is called distributed consensus; Raft and Paxos are two well-known algorithms that solve it.

The proven-impossible question of whether a general algorithm could exist that reliably determines, for any given program and any given input, whether that program will eventually stop running or run forever — proven impossible by Alan Turing in 1936. A question with no such algorithm is called undecidable.

Splitting one dataset that has grown too large for a single machine into smaller pieces, called shards, spread across many machines, each holding a distinct subset of the data — also called horizontal partitioning.

Deliberately storing more than one copy of the same data on more than one machine, called replicas, so that the loss of any single machine doesn't mean the loss or unavailability of the data it held, and so more than one request can be served at once.
